title: Numbers 21–100 and Phone Numbers
objective: Say and understand numbers 21–100, and exchange phone numbers digit by digit with grouping pauses.
intro_md: [L1: In this lesson you learn the numbers 21–100 and how to say a phone number in English: digit by digit, in small groups. Careful: thirteen and thirty sound very similar — listen for the stress!]

new_vocabulary.example_sentence: Twenty-one students are in my class.
One hundred is ten times ten.

notes: TODO_audio: ex2 (thirteen, 1.0x), ex6 (phone number read-out with grouping pauses, 0.75x), ex7 dictation (2 plays), ex8 (Fifteen students are in my class., 1.0x), ex9 speaking model. Band map §15: L11 vocab=12 — nine number items (tens pattern + one hundred + twenty-one as the composition exemplar), number, phone number, and the question chunk. Compound numbers 22-99 are composed from taught tens + L04 units, not stored as separate items.

exercises.prompt: twenty-one · thirty · forty · fifty · sixty · seventy · eighty · ninety · one hundred
exercises.rationale: The tens are the anchor forms: 22-99 are composed, not memorized, so these nine cards plus the L04 units cover the whole range.
P1 word-stress discrimination on the highest-value number pair; mishearing teen/ty wrecks phone numbers, times and prices in real life.

options.label: Thirteen.
options.rationale: Stress on the second syllable: thir-TEEN.

options.label: Thirty.
options.rationale: Stress on the first syllable: THIR-ty — the classic pair; listeners using vowel length alone (es/vi) fall here.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Match the figures to the words.]
exercises.rationale: Makes the composition rule visible: tens word + hyphen + unit word maps onto the two digits; 91 checks the rule where es composition differs (noventa y uno).
Sequence retrieval of the tens with the teen look-alikes as written distractors — the same trap as ex2, now in production.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Put the words in order to make the question.]
exercises.rationale: Builds the new chunk on the What's-your-X frame from L03; predicted error is 'number phone' (es noun order: número de teléfono) — feedback names the noun-noun order.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 0.75x] 'My phone number is five five five, two eight, nine one.' — [L1: Which number do you write?]
exercises.rationale: Digit-by-digit capture with grouping pauses is the lesson's real-world task; the distractors are the two most common capture failures.

options.rationale: Three groups with pauses: five five five — two eight — nine one.
One digit off in the middle group: catches listeners who stop checking after the first group.
Last two digits reversed: catches holding digits as a pair without their order.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 2 plays: 0.75x then 1.0x] 'My phone number is five five zero, nine two.'
exercises.key: My phone number is five five zero, nine two.
exercises.scoring: case-insensitive; digits accepted for the number words; comma optional
exercises.rationale: Sound-to-spelling for the possessive frame plus a digit string; zero is included because learners often only know 'oh' receptively.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 1.0x] 'Fifteen students are in my class.' — [L1: How many students?]
exercises.rationale: The teen/ty stress contrast embedded in a full sentence at natural speed — harder than ex2's isolated word, and recycles L07 vocabulary.

options.rationale: fif-TEEN: final-syllable stress marks the teen.
FIF-ty: initial stress — the mirror error of ex2, now under sentence prosody.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Say your phone number digit by digit, in small groups, with a short pause between groups.]
asr_focus: teen/ty stress if the number contains 13-19 or tens
exercises.rationale: Personalized production of the target routine; pause placement is what makes a number copyable by a listener, so ASR checks rhythm, not just digits.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Exchange phone numbers with the AI: ask with What's your phone number?, write down its answer, say your own number digit by digit, and repeat the AI's number back to check it.]
exercises.rationale: The §2 objective verbatim — exchange phone numbers; the repeat-back move forces both comprehension and production of digit strings in one exchange.
